equilibrium-concentrations-s3.title: Two students solve the same problem

For 2 H2S(g) ⇌ 2 H2(g) + S2(g), Kc = 1.0 × 10−6 at a certain temperature. A flask starts with 0.10 M H2S only.

Student P writes the Equilibrium row as [H2S] = 0.10 − 2x, [H2] = 2x, [S2] = x, assumes 2x is small next to 0.10, and writes (2x)2(x) / (0.10)2 = 1.0 × 10−6.

Student Q writes the same Equilibrium row, then drops x everywhere it appears, including the top: (0)2(0) / (0.10)2 = 1.0 × 10−6, and says there is no solution.

items.q: What belongs in the Change row for H<sub>2</sub>?
options: −x

items.q: Calculate [H<sub>2</sub>] at equilibrium.

mistakes.why: Value: you subtracted [NH₃] directly. 2x = 0.150 M gives x = 0.0750 M, and H₂ falls by 3x.
Value: H₂ falls by 3x, not x. Its coefficient is 3.
Value: x is half of [NH₃], because NH₃ rises by 2x. Use x = 0.0750 M.

items.q: Using the completed ICE table, calculate K<sub>c</sub> for ammonia formation at this temperature.

mistakes.why: Value: [H₂] must be cubed, because its coefficient is 3.
Value: you used the initial concentrations of N₂ and H₂. Use the equilibrium values from the ICE table.

items.q: Why does the Change row use one unknown, x, for all three species?
options: The coefficients fix the ratio of the changes.
The three concentrations change by equal amounts.
x is the equilibrium concentration of each species.
The volume is 1.00 L, so moles and molarity are equal.

items.q: Is the student’s small-x approximation valid?
options: No: 0.089 M is about 45% of 0.200 M, far more than 5%.
Yes: x comes out less than 0.200 M.
Yes: K = 0.040 is less than 1.
No: the approximation is not used when the products start at zero.

items.q: Solve x<sup>2</sup> / (0.200 − x) = 0.040 exactly (with the quadratic formula) and give [Cl<sub>2</sub>] at equilibrium.

mistakes.why: Value: that is the small-x answer, which is invalid here (45% of 0.200). Solve x² + 0.040x − 0.0080 = 0 exactly.
Value: you took the negative root. A concentration cannot be negative; use the positive root.

items.q: Using the exact x, calculate [PCl<sub>5</sub>] at equilibrium.

mistakes.why: Value: you used the small-x value of 0.089 M. Use the exact x = 0.072 M.
Value: [PCl₅] falls by x as it decomposes. Subtract x from 0.200 M.

items.q: Check: put the exact equilibrium concentrations back into the K expression. What should you get, and what does it confirm?
options: About 0.040, so Q = K.
About 0.089, confirming the approximation was valid.
Exactly 0.200, the starting concentration.
A value less than 0.040, showing the reaction is still going forward.

items.q: Which student used the small-x approximation correctly?
options: Student P, who drops x just from (0.10 − 2x).
Student Q, who sets each x term to zero because x is small.
Both, because dropping x anywhere gives the same approximation.
Neither, because the approximation works for two-species reactions.

items.q: Finish Student P’s calculation: find [S<sub>2</sub>] at equilibrium.

mistakes.why: Value: (2x)² = 4x², so the top is 4x³. Divide by 4 before taking the cube root.
Value: the top is 4x³, so take a cube root, not a square root.
Value: that is [H₂] = 2x. [S₂] is x.

items.q: How should Student P check that the approximation was justified?
options: Compare 2x with 0.10 M; it is under 5%.
Check that x is positive.
Check that K is less than 1.
Compare x with K; x should be smaller than K.

items.q: Why was it reasonable to expect x to be small before solving?
options: K = 1.0 × 10<sup>−6</sup> is very small.
The flask starts with no H<sub>2</sub> or S<sub>2</sub>.
H<sub>2</sub>S has a coefficient of 2 in the balanced equation.
The starting concentration, 0.10 M, is less than 1 M.

items.q: For H<sub>2</sub>(g) + I<sub>2</sub>(g) ⇌ 2 HI(g), K<sub>c</sub> = 50.0 at 450 °C. A flask starts with 0.100 M H<sub>2</sub> and 0.100 M I<sub>2</sub>. Calculate [HI] at equilibrium.

mistakes.why: Value: that is x. [HI] = 2x.
Value: you dropped x from 0.100 − x. K is not small here, so take the square root of both sides instead: 2x / (0.100 − x) = √50.0.
Value: that is [H₂] (0.100 − x), not [HI].

items.q: For 2 NOCl(g) ⇌ 2 NO(g) + Cl<sub>2</sub>(g), K<sub>c</sub> = 1.6 × 10<sup>−5</sup>. A flask starts with 0.50 M NOCl. Using the small-x approximation, calculate [Cl<sub>2</sub>] at equilibrium.

mistakes.why: Value: (2x)²x = 4x³. Divide by 4 before taking the cube root.
Value: that is [NO] = 2x. [Cl₂] = x.
Value: the top is 4x³, so take a cube root.

items.q: For CO(g) + H<sub>2</sub>O(g) ⇌ CO<sub>2</sub>(g) + H<sub>2</sub>(g), K<sub>c</sub> = 1.56. A flask starts with 0.0500 M CO, 0.0500 M H<sub>2</sub>O, 0.200 M CO<sub>2</sub> and 0.200 M H<sub>2</sub>. How should the Change row be written?
options: +x for CO, H<sub>2</sub>O; −x for CO<sub>2</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>
−x for CO, H<sub>2</sub>O; +x for CO<sub>2</sub>, H<sub>2</sub>
−x for each of the four species
0 for each species, since the four start at nonzero values

items.q: Continue the CO + H<sub>2</sub>O problem (K<sub>c</sub> = 1.56; start 0.0500 M CO, 0.0500 M H<sub>2</sub>O, 0.200 M CO<sub>2</sub>, 0.200 M H<sub>2</sub>). Calculate [CO] at equilibrium.

mistakes.why: Value: the net reaction runs in reverse, so CO increases: [CO] = 0.0500 + x.
Value: that is x. Add it to the starting 0.0500 M CO.

items.q: Put the steps for finding equilibrium concentrations from K in order.
options: Calculate Q from the starting concentrations and compare it with K to find the direction.
Set up the ICE table with the changes as x times the coefficients, signed for that direction.
Substitute the Equilibrium row into the K expression; simplify if x is small or the expression is a perfect square.
Solve for x, check it (5% rule, or substitute back), and calculate each concentration.

items.q: In which case is the small-x approximation most likely to be valid?
options: K = 2 × 10<sup>−8</sup>, start at 0.50 M
K = 2 × 10<sup>−1</sup>, start at 0.010 M
K = 5 × 10<sup>3</sup>, start at 1.0 M
K = 1.0, start at 0.10 M

items.q: For a reaction A(g) ⇌ B(g) + C(g), K<sub>c</sub> = 4.0 × 10<sup>−4</sup>. Starting from 0.100 M A, the small-x approximation gives x = 6.3 × 10<sup>−3</sup> M. Calculate the percent of A that reacts.

mistakes.why: Value: that is x itself. Divide x by 0.100 M and multiply by 100%.

items.q: For the reaction in the previous calculation, x / [A]<sub>0</sub> came out at 6.3%. What should the student do?
options: Solve exactly; x is over 5% of 0.100 M.
Keep the approximate answer, because 6.3% is less than 10%.
Change K to make x smaller.
Double x to account for the error.

items.q: A flask of A(g) ⇌ B(g) + C(g) (K<sub>c</sub> small) starts with 0.20 M A instead of 0.10 M A, at the same temperature. Predict each quantity at equilibrium, compared with the 0.10 M flask.
What is the earliest time shown at which the system is at equilibrium?
options: 0 s

items.q: Calculate [W] at equilibrium.

mistakes.why: Value: 0.40 mol is the amount. Divide by the 2.0 L volume to get molarity.
Value: 4 is the particle count. Each particle is 0.10 mol, and the volume is 2.0 L.

items.q: Calculate K<sub>c</sub> for 2 W(g) ⇌ W<sub>2</sub>(g).

mistakes.why: Value: you used particle counts. Because the moles of gas differ on the two sides, counts and concentrations give different K values; convert to molarity first.
Value: [W] is squared, because its coefficient is 2.
Value: you used moles, not concentrations. Divide each amount by 2.0 L.

items.q: Between 0 s and 20 s, which statement about the rates is correct?
options: The forward rate is greater than the reverse rate.
The rates are equal.
The reverse rate is greater than the forward rate.
Both rates are zero at 0 s.

items.q: A student calculates K by using the particle counts directly: K = 4 / 4<sup>2</sup> = 0.25. Why does this differ from K<sub>c</sub>?
options: K<sub>c</sub> needs mol/L, and the volume does not cancel here.
Counts are not allowed in K, because particles are too small to count.
The student should have counted W<sub>2</sub> as two particles.
K depends on the number of particles drawn, so both answers are valid.

items.q: Which boxes show mixtures at equilibrium? Select all that apply.
options: Box 1
Box 2
Box 3
Box 4

items.q: How will the contents of Box 3 change as it approaches equilibrium?
options: XY will decrease, because Q > K.
XY will increase, because Q > K.
Nothing will change, because XY is the most abundant species.
X<sub>2</sub> will decrease, because there is very little of it.

items.q: Box 2 reaches equilibrium. Which set of counts could it then show?
options: 2 X<sub>2</sub>, 2 Y<sub>2</sub>, 4 XY
3 X<sub>2</sub>, 3 Y<sub>2</sub>, 4 XY
4 X<sub>2</sub>, 4 Y<sub>2</sub>, 0 XY
1 X<sub>2</sub>, 1 Y<sub>2</sub>, 6 XY

items.q: Why can particle counts be used directly in Q for this reaction?
options: The gas moles are equal on both sides, so the volume cancels.
Counts and concentrations are the same thing in any reaction.
The containers are drawn the same size.
K is 4.0, which is a whole number.

items.q: Use the graph to calculate K<sub>c</sub>.

mistakes.why: Value: [B] is squared in K, because its coefficient is 2.
Value: you inverted K. Products go on top.
Value: read the plateau values, after the curves level off, not a point on the way.

items.q: How does the graph show that B forms twice as fast as A is used up?
options: [B] rises by 0.80 M while [A] falls by 0.40 M.
[B] ends twice as high as [A].
Both curves level off at the same time.
[B] starts at zero.

items.q: A student says the system reaches equilibrium at about 18 s, where the curves cross. Which response is best?
options: Wrong: equilibrium is where the curves level off, not where they cross.
Right: equal concentrations mean equal rates.
Right: after the crossing, B is favored, so the reaction stops.
Wrong: equilibrium is not reached, because the curves do not meet again.

items.q: Calculate Q<sub>c</sub> at 10 s, when [A] = 0.62 M and [B] = 0.36 M.

mistakes.why: Value: square [B]; its coefficient is 2.

items.q: In a particle diagram of a system at equilibrium, what is true about two diagrams of the same container drawn at later times?
options: They show the same numbers of each kind of particle.
They show product particles and no reactants.
They show equal numbers of reactant and product particles.
They show the particles in the same positions.

items.q: Put the steps for finding K<sub>c</sub> from a particle diagram in order.
options: Confirm the diagram shows equilibrium (counts unchanged over time).
Count each kind of particle.
Convert counts to moles, then divide by the volume to get molarity.
Substitute the molarities into the K<sub>c</sub> expression.

items.q: What change was made at 50 s?
options: Cl<sub>2</sub> was added.
PCl<sub>5</sub> was added.
The temperature was raised.
The volume was halved.

items.q: Which statement describes the response after 50 s?
options: The net reaction runs in reverse, using some of the added Cl<sub>2</sub>.
The net reaction runs forward, making more Cl<sub>2</sub>.
There is no net reaction, because K has not changed.
The net reaction runs in reverse until [Cl<sub>2</sub>] is back to its old value.

items.q: At the new equilibrium, [PCl<sub>3</sub>] = 0.039 M. Calculate the new [PCl<sub>5</sub>].

mistakes.why: Value: the reverse reaction makes PCl₅, so [PCl₅] goes up by the same amount [PCl₃] goes down.
Value: [PCl₅] changes during the shift. Add the amount of PCl₃ that reacted.

items.q: How does K<sub>c</sub> after 100 s compare with K<sub>c</sub> before 50 s?
options: It is the same, 0.040.
It is larger, because more Cl<sub>2</sub> is present.
It is smaller, because the reaction shifted in reverse.
It is undefined until the added Cl<sub>2</sub> is used up.

items.q: Compare the new equilibrium (after 100 s) with the original equilibrium (before 50 s).
What do tubes 2 and 3 show about the forward reaction?
options: It is endothermic.
It is exothermic.
It is faster when cold.
It does not depend on temperature.

items.q: Why does tube 5 turn pink?
options: Ag<sup>+</sup> removes Cl<sup>−</sup> as AgCl(s).
Ag<sup>+</sup> adds to the blue ion, turning it pink.
Adding a solution dilutes the tube, which turns it pink.
NO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup> reacts with the pink ion.

items.q: How does K<sub>c</sub> in tube 2 compare with K<sub>c</sub> in tube 1?
options: Greater: higher T, endothermic forward reaction.
The same, because no substance was added.
Smaller, because the reaction shifted toward the products.
The same, because K is a constant.

items.q: In tube 4, why does the solution turn blue?
options: Added Cl<sup>−</sup> shifts the equilibrium forward.
HCl raises the temperature of the solution.
Added Cl<sup>−</sup> increases K.
HCl removes water, the product.

items.q: For N<sub>2</sub>(g) + 3 H<sub>2</sub>(g) ⇌ 2 NH<sub>3</sub>(g), ΔH° = −92 kJ/mol<sub>rxn</sub>, at equilibrium in a sealed container. Predict how the amount of NH<sub>3</sub> at the new equilibrium compares with before each change.

variables.name: The volume of the container is halved

items.q: For H<sub>2</sub>(g) + I<sub>2</sub>(g) ⇌ 2 HI(g) at equilibrium in a sealed container fitted with a movable piston, predict the effect on the amount of HI.

variables.name: The volume is doubled at constant temperature
Argon is added at constant volume

items.q: For 2 SO<sub>2</sub>(g) + O<sub>2</sub>(g) ⇌ 2 SO<sub>3</sub>(g), ΔH° = −198 kJ/mol<sub>rxn</sub>, which change increases the value of K?
options: Cooling the mixture
Adding more O<sub>2</sub>
Decreasing the volume
Adding a catalyst

items.q: For N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub>(g) ⇌ 2 NO<sub>2</sub>(g), the volume of an equilibrium mixture is suddenly halved at constant temperature. What happens to the brown color?
options: It darkens at once, then fades partway.
It fades at once, because the system shifts toward N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub>.
It darkens and stays at that darker shade.
It does not change, because K does not change.

items.q: For C(s) + H<sub>2</sub>O(g) ⇌ CO(g) + H<sub>2</sub>(g), ΔH° = +131 kJ/mol<sub>rxn</sub>, which changes shift the equilibrium toward the products? Select all that apply.
options: Raising the temperature
Increasing the volume
Adding more C(s)
Adding a catalyst

items.q: A student explains: "Adding more N<sub>2</sub> to the ammonia equilibrium makes K bigger, so more NH<sub>3</sub> forms." What is wrong with this explanation?
options: K is unchanged; the added N<sub>2</sub> upsets the equilibrium.
Nothing is wrong; adding a reactant raises K.
Adding N<sub>2</sub> makes K smaller, so less NH<sub>3</sub> forms.
Adding N<sub>2</sub> has no effect, because N<sub>2</sub> is unreactive.

items.q: Which statement correctly justifies the shift after change A?
options: Q > K, so the net reaction goes in reverse.
K increases because NO<sub>2</sub> was added, so the system shifts forward.
The reverse reaction speeds up, so the system shifts toward NO<sub>2</sub>.
Q < K, so the net reaction goes forward.

items.q: After change B (volume doubled), which way does the system shift and why?
options: Forward: halving each concentration halves Q.
No shift, because both concentrations were halved equally.
In reverse, because a larger volume favors fewer gas moles.
Forward, because doubling the volume doubles K.

items.q: After change C, what happens to [NO<sub>2</sub>] as the system returns to equilibrium?
options: It decreases, because Q > K and the net reaction runs in reverse.
It increases, because Q > K and the net reaction runs forward.
It stays the same, because NO<sub>2</sub> was not changed.
It increases, because the removed N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub> is replaced by NO<sub>2</sub>.

items.q: In another experiment, starting from the original equilibrium mixture, some NO<sub>2</sub> is removed so that [NO<sub>2</sub>] = 0.0100 M while [N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub>] stays 0.0400 M. Calculate Q<sub>c</sub> right after the change.

mistakes.why: Value: [NO₂] must be squared, because its coefficient is 2.
Value: you inverted Q. Products go on top.

items.q: In a fourth experiment, the flask is heated. The reaction is endothermic. How should the shift be justified?
options: K rises, so now Q < K: net forward.
Q increases with temperature, so the mixture shifts in reverse.
K stays the same, but the forward rate increases, so it shifts forward.
Heat is a product, so the system shifts in reverse.

items.q: Using particle counts (the gas moles are equal on both sides), calculate K for this reaction.

mistakes.why: Value: [XY] is squared, because its coefficient is 2.

items.q: Which justification of the shift after X<sub>2</sub> is added would earn full credit?
options: Q = 4²/(5 × 2) = 1.6 < K = 4.0, so net forward until Q = K.
Adding X<sub>2</sub> to the container increases K, so more XY forms.
The system wants to use up the extra X<sub>2</sub>, so it shifts right.
Adding X<sub>2</sub> speeds up the forward reaction, so it shifts right.

items.q: Compared with the left container, how do the amounts in the right container compare once equilibrium is restored?
options: More X<sub>2</sub>, less Y<sub>2</sub>, more XY
The same amounts of each as in the left container
Less X<sub>2</sub>, more Y<sub>2</sub> and less XY than the left container
More X<sub>2</sub>, the same Y<sub>2</sub> and the same XY as the left container

items.q: Immediately after the X<sub>2</sub> is added, which rate has changed?
options: The forward rate has increased.
The reverse rate has increased.
Both rates have increased equally.
Neither rate has changed.

items.q: CaCO<sub>3</sub>(s) ⇌ CaO(s) + CO<sub>2</sub>(g) is at equilibrium in a sealed container. Some CO<sub>2</sub> is pumped out at constant temperature. Which justification is correct?
options: Q = P<sub>CO₂</sub> drops below K<sub>p</sub>, so more CaCO<sub>3</sub> decomposes until P<sub>CO₂</sub> returns to K<sub>p</sub>.
K<sub>p</sub> drops, so the system shifts in reverse.
There is no shift, because the solids are unchanged.
Q rises above K<sub>p</sub>, so CO<sub>2</sub> is used up.

items.q: For N<sub>2</sub>(g) + 3 H<sub>2</sub>(g) ⇌ 2 NH<sub>3</sub>(g) at equilibrium, the volume is suddenly halved at constant temperature. By what factor does Q change at that instant? (Give Q<sub>new</sub> / Q<sub>old</sub>.)

mistakes.why: Value: every concentration doubles. The top has (2)² and the bottom (2)(2)³ = 16, so Q changes by 4/16.
Value: you only counted the top. The bottom grows by 2 × 2³ = 16, so Q falls to 4/16 of its value.

items.q: For an exothermic reaction at equilibrium, the temperature is lowered. Which statement is correct?
options: K increases, so Q < K: shift to products.
K decreases; Q > K, so it shifts toward reactants.
K stays the same; Q decreases, so it shifts toward products.
Neither Q nor K changes, so there is no shift.

items.q: Which statements are valid justifications on a free-response question? Select all that apply.
options: "Adding H<sub>2</sub> makes Q < K, so the net reaction proceeds forward until Q = K."
"Raising the temperature increases K for this endothermic reaction, so Q < K and the reaction shifts forward."
"Adding H<sub>2</sub> increases K, so more product forms."
"The reaction shifts right to relieve the stress."

items.q: For 2 SO<sub>2</sub>(g) + O<sub>2</sub>(g) ⇌ 2 SO<sub>3</sub>(g), K<sub>c</sub> = 280. A mixture has Q = 280. Then SO<sub>2</sub> and SO<sub>3</sub> are both doubled in concentration at constant temperature, with O<sub>2</sub> unchanged. What happens?
options: No shift, since Q is still 280.
Forward shift: more reactant was added.
Reverse shift: more product was added.
K doubles, so the system shifts forward.

items.q: Put the parts of a full-credit justification for an equilibrium shift in order.
options: State what the change does to Q (or to K, if the temperature changed).
Compare the new Q with K, giving the inequality.
State the direction of the net reaction that follows from the comparison.
State that the reaction continues until Q = K again.

items.q: Calculate the molar solubility of AgCl in pure water at 25 °C.

mistakes.why: Value: s² = K<sub>sp</sub>, so take the square root; do not divide by 2.
Value: AgCl gives one ion of each kind, so K<sub>sp</sub> = s², not 4s³.

items.q: Calculate the molar solubility of Ag<sub>2</sub>CrO<sub>4</sub> in pure water at 25 °C.

mistakes.why: Value: Ag₂CrO₄ gives 2 Ag⁺ per formula unit. K<sub>sp</sub> = (2s)²(s) = 4s³; take a cube root.
Value: you wrote 2s² × s. The silver concentration 2s must be squared as a whole: (2s)² = 4s².
Value: (2s)² = 4s², so K<sub>sp</sub> = 4s³. Divide by 4 before the cube root.

items.q: Ag<sub>2</sub>CrO<sub>4</sub> has a smaller K<sub>sp</sub> than AgCl. Which salt has the greater molar solubility in water?
options: Ag<sub>2</sub>CrO<sub>4</sub>
AgCl
They are equally soluble, because both are silver salts.
It is undecided without the masses of the salts.

items.q: Which pair of salts can be ranked by solubility just by comparing their K<sub>sp</sub> values?
options: AgCl and AgBr
AgCl and Ag<sub>2</sub>CrO<sub>4</sub>
AgBr and CaF<sub>2</sub>
Ag<sub>2</sub>CrO<sub>4</sub> and AgBr

items.q: Calculate [F<sup>−</sup>] in a saturated solution of CaF<sub>2</sub> in water at 25 °C.

mistakes.why: Value: that is s, the molar solubility. Each CaF₂ gives two F⁻, so [F⁻] = 2s.
Value: CaF₂ gives 1 Ca²⁺ and 2 F⁻, so K<sub>sp</sub> = s(2s)² = 4s³.

items.q: What is the formula of the salt?
options: MX<sub>2</sub>
MX
M<sub>2</sub>X
M<sub>3</sub>X<sub>6</sub>

items.q: Use the diagram to calculate K<sub>sp</sub> for the salt.

mistakes.why: Value: [X⁻] is squared, because each MX₂ gives two X⁻ (coefficient 2).
Value: square [X⁻] rather than doubling it.
Value: you used particle counts. Convert each count to a concentration first (× 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ M).

items.q: More solid MX<sub>2</sub> is added to the beaker and stirred at 25 °C. What happens to the number of dissolved ions?
options: It stays the same, because the solution is already saturated and the solid is not in K<sub>sp</sub>.
It increases, because more solid is available to dissolve.
It decreases, because the extra solid pulls ions out of solution.
It doubles, because the amount of solid doubled.

items.q: Which statement describes the particles in this beaker?
options: Ions leave the solid and ions return to it at equal rates.
No more ions dissolve, because the solution is full.
Ions dissolve, but ions no longer return to the solid.
The solid and the ions no longer interact.

items.q: A saturated solution of PbI<sub>2</sub> (molar mass 461.0 g/mol) contains 0.62 g of dissolved PbI<sub>2</sub> per liter at 25 °C. Calculate K<sub>sp</sub>.

mistakes.why: Value: PbI₂ gives two I⁻, so K<sub>sp</sub> = s(2s)² = 4s³.
Value: square the whole [I⁻] = 2s: (2s)² = 4s².
Value: convert grams per liter to moles per liter first, using the molar mass.

items.q: The molar solubility of Mg(OH)<sub>2</sub> in water at 25 °C is 1.1 × 10<sup>−4</sup> M. Calculate K<sub>sp</sub>.

mistakes.why: Value: you did not square [OH⁻]. K<sub>sp</sub> = [Mg²⁺][OH⁻]² = s(2s)².
Value: [OH⁻] is 2s, not s. Each Mg(OH)₂ gives two OH⁻.
Value: Mg(OH)₂ is not a 1 : 1 salt. Use [OH⁻] = 2s and square it.

items.q: Which is the K<sub>sp</sub> expression for Ca<sub>3</sub>(PO<sub>4</sub>)<sub>2</sub>(s) ⇌ 3 Ca<sup>2+</sup>(aq) + 2 PO<sub>4</sub><sup>3−</sup>(aq)?
options: [Ca<sup>2+</sup>]<sup>3</sup>[PO<sub>4</sub><sup>3−</sup>]<sup>2</sup>
[Ca<sup>2+</sup>]<sup>3</sup>[PO<sub>4</sub><sup>3−</sup>]<sup>2</sup> / [Ca<sub>3</sub>(PO<sub>4</sub>)<sub>2</sub>]
3[Ca<sup>2+</sup>] × 2[PO<sub>4</sub><sup>3−</sup>]
[Ca<sup>2+</sup>][PO<sub>4</sub><sup>3−</sup>]

items.q: Equal volumes of 2.0 × 10<sup>−4</sup> M AgNO<sub>3</sub> and 2.0 × 10<sup>−4</sup> M NaCl are mixed. K<sub>sp</sub> of AgCl is 1.8 × 10<sup>−10</sup>. Does AgCl precipitate?
options: Yes: Q = 1.0 × 10<sup>−8</sup> > K<sub>sp</sub>.
No: Q = 1.0 × 10<sup>−8</sup> < K<sub>sp</sub>.
Yes: Q = 4.0 × 10<sup>−8</sup> > K<sub>sp</sub>.
No: both solutions are too dilute to form a solid.

items.q: Put the steps for finding molar solubility from K<sub>sp</sub> in order.
options: Write the dissolving equation, with the ions in the ratio of the formula.
Let s be the molar solubility and write each ion concentration as s times its coefficient.
Write K<sub>sp</sub> with each ion concentration raised to its coefficient, e.g. s(2s)<sup>2</sup> = 4s<sup>3</sup>.
Solve for s and report it in mol/L.

items.q: The dissolving of a salt in water is endothermic. A saturated solution with excess solid is warmed. What happens?
options: More solid dissolves, because K<sub>sp</sub> increases.
Solid precipitates, because K<sub>sp</sub> increases.
Nothing, because K<sub>sp</sub> is a constant.
More solid dissolves, because Q increases.

items.q: K<sub>sp</sub> of Ca(OH)<sub>2</sub> is 5.0 × 10<sup>−6</sup> at 25 °C. Calculate [OH<sup>−</sup>] in a saturated solution.

mistakes.why: Value: that is s, the molar solubility. Each Ca(OH)₂ gives two OH⁻, so [OH⁻] = 2s.
Value: Ca(OH)₂ gives three ions, so K<sub>sp</sub> = s(2s)² = 4s³; use a cube root.
Value: (2s)² = 4s², so K<sub>sp</sub> = 4s³, not 2s³.

items.q: The molar solubility of Ag<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>4</sub> in water is 4.3 × 10<sup>−5</sup> M at 25 °C. Calculate K<sub>sp</sub>.

mistakes.why: Value: [Ag⁺] = 3s must be cubed as a whole: (3s)³ = 27s³.
Value: [Ag⁺] is 3s, not s. K<sub>sp</sub> = (3s)³(s) = 27s⁴.
Value: raise [Ag⁺] = 3s to the power 3, its coefficient: K<sub>sp</sub> = (3s)³(s).

items.q: K<sub>sp</sub> of BaSO<sub>4</sub> (molar mass 233.39 g/mol) is 1.1 × 10<sup>−10</sup> at 25 °C. Calculate the mass of BaSO<sub>4</sub> that dissolves in 1.00 L of water.

mistakes.why: Value: that is the molar solubility in mol/L. Multiply by 1.00 L and by the molar mass to get grams.
Value: take the square root of K<sub>sp</sub> first; K<sub>sp</sub> = s² for a 1 : 1 salt.

items.q: A saturated solution of AgCl is in contact with excess solid at 25 °C. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.
options: [Ag<sup>+</sup>] = [Cl<sup>−</sup>] if no other source of either ion is present.
Adding more water and stirring dissolves more solid, but [Ag<sup>+</sup>] ends up the same.
K<sub>sp</sub> is larger when more solid is present.
No AgCl dissolves once the solution is saturated.

items.q: What trend does the table show?
options: PbCl<sub>2</sub> is less soluble when more Cl<sup>−</sup> is already in solution.
PbCl<sub>2</sub> is more soluble in salt solutions than in water.
The solubility of PbCl<sub>2</sub> does not depend on [NaCl].
PbCl<sub>2</sub> is less soluble because K<sub>sp</sub> decreases in salt solutions.

items.q: Which explanation of the trend would earn credit?
options: Cl<sup>−</sup> from NaCl raises Q, so less PbCl<sub>2</sub> dissolves before Q = K<sub>sp</sub>.
NaCl lowers K<sub>sp</sub> for PbCl<sub>2</sub>.
Na<sup>+</sup> ions react with Pb<sup>2+</sup> and remove it.
NaCl takes up the water, leaving less for PbCl<sub>2</sub> to dissolve in.

items.q: Using the small-x approximation ([Cl<sup>−</sup>] ≈ 0.25 M), calculate the molar solubility of PbCl<sub>2</sub> in 0.25 M NaCl.

mistakes.why: Value: you divided K<sub>sp</sub> by 0.25 (or by 4 × 0.0625). [Cl⁻] ≈ 0.25 M is squared and not multiplied by 4: s = K<sub>sp</sub> / (0.25)².
Value: that is the solubility in pure water. Include the 0.25 M Cl⁻ from NaCl.

items.q: A student uses the small-x approximation for 0.010 M NaCl and gets s = 1.7 × 10<sup>−1</sup> M. What went wrong?
options: 2s is not small next to 0.010 M.
The student forgot to square [Cl<sup>−</sup>].
K<sub>sp</sub> should be multiplied by 4.
Nothing; a smaller [Cl<sup>−</sup>] means a larger solubility.

items.q: A saturated solution of PbCl<sub>2</sub> with excess solid is at 25 °C. Solid NaCl is dissolved in it. Predict each quantity after equilibrium is restored.
Calculate the molar solubility of Ag<sub>2</sub>CrO<sub>4</sub> in beaker 2.

mistakes.why: Value: [Ag⁺] is squared in K<sub>sp</sub>: s = K<sub>sp</sub> / (0.050)².
Value: [Ag⁺] ≈ 0.050 M from AgNO₃; it is not doubled. The 2 in 2s applies only to Ag⁺ coming from the dissolving salt.
Value: that is the solubility in pure water; include the Ag⁺ already present.

items.q: Calculate the molar solubility of Ag<sub>2</sub>CrO<sub>4</sub> in beaker 3.

mistakes.why: Value: that is [Ag⁺] = 2s. Divide by 2 to get s.
Value: K<sub>sp</sub> = (2s)²(0.050), so (2s)² = K<sub>sp</sub>/0.050; take a square root.
Value: (2s)² = 4s². Solve 4s² = K<sub>sp</sub>/0.050.

items.q: Rank the molar solubility of Ag<sub>2</sub>CrO<sub>4</sub> in the three beakers, from greatest to least.
How does K<sub>sp</sub> of Ag<sub>2</sub>CrO<sub>4</sub> in beaker 2 compare with its value in beaker 1?
options: It is the same.
It is smaller, because less solid dissolves.
It is larger, because [Ag<sup>+</sup>] is larger.
It is undefined, because Ag<sup>+</sup> comes from two sources.

items.q: K<sub>sp</sub> of AgCl is 1.8 × 10<sup>−10</sup>. Calculate its molar solubility in 0.020 M CaCl<sub>2</sub>.

mistakes.why: Value: each CaCl₂ gives two Cl⁻, so [Cl⁻] = 0.040 M, not 0.020 M.
Value: that is the solubility in pure water. Include the Cl⁻ from CaCl₂.

items.q: By what factor is the solubility of AgCl (K<sub>sp</sub> = 1.8 × 10<sup>−10</sup>) lower in 0.10 M NaCl than in pure water? (Give s<sub>water</sub> / s<sub>NaCl</sub>.)

mistakes.why: Value: you divided the other way. s in water is the larger value.

items.q: Which added solutes would lower the solubility of CaF<sub>2</sub> in water? Select all that apply.
options: NaF
NaCl
KNO<sub>3</sub>
Sugar (C<sub>12</sub>H<sub>22</sub>O<sub>11</sub>)

items.q: A saturated solution of BaSO<sub>4</sub> is at equilibrium with the solid. Concentrated Na<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> solution is added. Which statement gives the best justification of what happens?
options: Q rises above K<sub>sp</sub>, so BaSO<sub>4</sub> precipitates.
K<sub>sp</sub> rises because more sulfate is present, so more BaSO<sub>4</sub> dissolves.
Na<sup>+</sup> replaces Ba<sup>2+</sup> in the solid.
The reverse reaction speeds up, so the system shifts.

items.q: Put the steps for calculating solubility in a solution with a common ion in order.
options: Find the concentration of the common ion from the soluble salt (count its ions per formula unit).
Write each ion concentration: s times the coefficient, plus the common-ion concentration for the shared ion.
Approximate (common ion + small term) ≈ common ion, and solve K<sub>sp</sub> for s.
Check that the dropped term is under 5% of the common-ion concentration.

items.q: Why does adding a common ion lower solubility, at the particle level?
options: Ions rejoin the solid more often, so less salt dissolves before the rates match.
The added ions coat the surface of the solid so water does not reach it.
The added ions make the water less polar.
The added ions react with the solid to make a new compound.

items.q: K<sub>sp</sub> of Mg(OH)<sub>2</sub> is 5.6 × 10<sup>−12</sup>. Calculate [Mg<sup>2+</sup>] that can remain dissolved in a solution in which [OH<sup>−</sup>] is held at 1.0 × 10<sup>−3</sup> M.

mistakes.why: Value: [OH⁻] is squared: [Mg²⁺] = K<sub>sp</sub> / [OH⁻]².
Value: [OH⁻] is given directly as 1.0 × 10⁻³ M; do not double it.
